title: Serving runtime — architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling playbook, benchmarks & runbooks
author: Ava Thompson
content:
Overview

This document consolidates the serving runtime reference material: architecture overview, kernel scheduling design, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, recent release notes, known issues, and actionable runbooks for oncall and SRE teams. It is intended for engineers owning runtime performance, platform operators supporting Dedicated/Private deployments, and product engineers validating regressions.

1) Runtime architecture (high-level)

Summary:
- The serving runtime is a GPU-optimized inference engine designed for low-latency, high-throughput LLM serving across hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.
- Core components: request router, scheduler, batching layer, kernel selection, KV cache manager, model artifact manager, and telemetry/trace exporter.

Key design points:
- Continuous batching: requests are pooled per-model and per-variant with adaptive time windows to trade latency vs throughput.
- Hot/cold path segregation: short prompt, low-token-length requests are served with fast-path kernels; long-context requests use memory-optimized kernels with streaming.
- Kernel selection & compilation: the runtime selects pre-compiled kernels based on architecture + sequence-length histogram. Kernel cache is persisted on local NVMe for quick startup.
- KV cache and prefix caching: per-session KV cache can be pinned or evicted per policy; prefix reuse is detected by the router to serve from cache when possible.
- Smart routing: policy rules route requests to hosted, dedicated, or fallback variants depending on latency SLO, cost budget, and regional capacity.

Operational SLOs (examples):
- P95 token generation latency (small models, <=512 tokens): < 150 ms
- Tail-latency mitigation: p99 < 450 ms for provisioned Dedicated pools (default policy)
- Throughput per GPU (A100 80GB): 120 tokens/s sustained for gpt-like-7B quantized workloads (baseline)
- Error rate SLO: < 0.1% 5xx per 24h window

2) Kernel scheduling and execution model

Goals:
- Maximize GPU utilization while respecting per-request latency SLOs and isolation between tenants.

Scheduling primitives:
- Queues: each model variant has 3 priority queues (real-time, standard, background). Real-time is rate limited and sized for strict-latency requests.
- Batching windows: dynamic batching windows use an adaptive timeout (configurable; default 4ms) and token-capacity thresholds.
- Time-slicing & preemption: long-running kernels (long-context or sampling with many tokens) are cooperative and yield at per-layer boundaries. Short jobs can preempt background batches when real-time queue length exceeds threshold.
- GPU-resident kernel pool: kernels are cached in GPU memory where possible. Eviction policy is LRU with pinning for high-traffic variants.

Isolation & fairness:
- Token-budget controller: per-tenant token budgets are enforced at router to ensure fairness during contention.
- Soft QoS: requests tagged premium bypass background queue up to a configured rate.
- Memory accounting: models expose a memory footprint annotation; scheduler uses it to bin-packing across GPU instances.

3) Profiling playbook (how to collect useful traces)

Purpose: determine root cause for latency regressions, OOMs, or throughput drops.

Step-by-step:
1. Reproduce in staging with representative workload (use the benchmark harness section below).
2. Enable distributed tracing (X-Request-Id + trace sampling 100%) on the staging route.
3. Collect GPU telemetry: nvidia-smi dmon, DCGM metrics, and per-process GPU usage (every 1s for 2 minutes).
4. Capture kernel-level profiles: run runtime with --profile-mode=kernel (produces per-kernel ms and memory). Example: ./runtime --profile-mode=kernel --profile-output=/tmp/run123.prof
5. Record host-level metrics: CPU, mem, disk IO, NVMe latency, and cgroup stats.
6. If OOM suspected, capture heap + device allocation traces: enable --alloc-trace and upload artifacts to /artifacts/profiles/<id>.
7. Analyze artifacts with profiler-ui (internal) or use the profiling script: python tools/analyze_profile.py /tmp/run123.prof --report /tmp/run123.html

Key metrics to inspect:
- avg and p95 per-kernel execution time
- batch formation latency (time between request arrival and kernel launch)
- queue lengths over time per-priority queue
- GPU SM utilization and memory fragmentation
- KV cache hit ratio and eviction frequency

Thresholds & alerts (recommended):
- batch formation latency > 10ms sustained for 30s -> page SRE
- p95 per-kernel exec time deviation > 3x baseline -> create regression issue
- GPU memory fragmentation leading to allocation retries > 5 in 60s -> schedule maintenance (warmup or reduce concurrency)

4) Benchmarking suite (CI + local)

Overview:
- The benchmarking suite measures latency/throughput across model sizes, quantization profiles, sequence lengths, and mixing workloads. Benchmarks are reproducible via Docker images stored in gcr.io/redwood-ci/serve-bench:latest.

Included tests:
- latency-p95-short: 1000 requests, seq=64, concurrency=16
- stream-latency: streaming token latency for 1k sessions, sample-rate=1
- throughput-sustained: 10m sustained run with concurrency ramp-up
- cold-start: measure cold-start time after model eviction from GPU

How to run locally (short example):
- docker run --rm -v $(pwd)/out:/out gcr.io/redwood-ci/serve-bench:latest "bench run --target localhost:8080 --test latency-p95-short --out /out/bench1.json"

CI integration:
- Benchmarks run nightly and before major runtime releases. Baselines stored in benchstore. A regression is flagged when p95 latency increases by > 15% or throughput drops by > 10%.
- PR gating: heavy benchmarks run in the release pipeline for changes touching kernel scheduler or kernel selection.

Artifacts & reproducibility:
- Each benchmark execution records: git sha, docker image digest, hardware profile, kernel library version, and input workload seed.
- Use bench-compare tool to diff runs: bench-compare --base benchstore/v1.8.0.json --new /out/bench1.json

5) Release notes (runtime v1.8.0 - 2026-03-01)

Highlights:
- Improved kernel selection logic to reduce cold-starts for long-context variants (28% cold-start reduction on A100 80GB).
- Adaptive batching timeout: default reduced from 6ms to 4ms with a new hysteresis mechanism. Expected p95 latency improvement of ~8% for small models.
- Kernel cache persistence on NVMe to speed model warmup after host reboots.
- New profiling flags: --profile-mode=kernel and --alloc-trace for detailed allocation traces.

Upgrade notes (operators):
1. Drain non-critical nodes: kubectl cordon/evict with label runtime=v1.7.x
2. Deploy runtime image redwood/runtime:v1.8.0 and confirm kernel-compiler image is present (gcr.io/redwood-ci/kernel-compiler:v20260224).
3. After the rollout, validate: bench run --target <node> --test cold-start (expect 20-30% improvement).
4. If any GPU kernel fails to load, roll back to v1.7.x and open a priority incident with runtime@redwood.com.

6) Known issues (summary)

- ISSUE-421: Intermittent p99 spikes on q4_8 quantized models under mixed workload. Workaround: pin q4_8 models to dedicated pools or reduce background concurrency.
- ISSUE-439: Rare CUDA library mismatch on Ubuntu 22.04 images when kernel-compiler version mismatched. Workaround: ensure kernel-compiler:v20260224 is used.
- ISSUE-452: NVMe eviction race leading to temporary model-load failures during high GC. Mitigation: schedule staggered model preloads during rolling upgrades.

7) Runtime runbooks (operational playbooks)

A) Latency spike - p95/p99 elevated
1. Check SLO dashboard and scope: identify affected model variants and regions.
2. Run the profiling collection commands (see profiling playbook).
3. Check queue lengths and batch formation latency in the last 5 minutes.
4. If batch formation latency is high: temporarily reduce batching window: set runtime config batching.timeout_ms=2 for the affected model route.
5. If a specific kernel shows high exec time: route traffic to compatible fallback variant (see routing policy) and create regression bug.
6. Notify product owner and post summary to #runtime-ops with trace links and bench artifacts.

B) OOM on node
1. Evict non-critical pods: kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data <node>
2. Collect alloc-trace artifact and upload.
3. Check memory accounting logs for model with largest footprint.
4. If memory fragmentation suspected, temporarily reduce concurrency via token-budget-controller and schedule node rebuild with kernel-cache warmup.

C) Model fails to load after upgrade
1. Confirm kernel-compiler image digest and CUDA driver version.
2. Check kernel loader logs: /var/log/runtime/kernel-loader.log for symbol mismatches.
3. If failure persists, rollback to previous runtime image and open an incident.

9) Maintenance & future work items

Planned items (quarterly roadmap):
- Add per-model adaptive batching policies driven by workload telemetry (Q2 2026).
- Improve memory defragmentation strategies in the allocator to reduce OOM incidents (Q3 2026).
- Tight integration with Redwood Console to expose kernel-level traces for customer-facing routes (Q4 2026).

Appendix: commands & snippets

1) Profiling example command:
- ./runtime --profile-mode=kernel --profile-output=/tmp/run.prof --log-level=info

2) Simple benchmark example:
- docker run --rm gcr.io/redwood-ci/serve-bench:latest bench run --target localhost:8080 --test latency-p95-short --out /out/bench1.json
